Have you ever been in a group chat?

Ten people talking directly to each other everyone messaging everyone. When someone changes their name, eight people need to update their contact. When someone leaves, everyone needs to know. The more people, the more chaos.
Now imagine a group admin. Nobody talks to each other directly. Everyone sends their message to the admin, and the admin decides who gets notified and what happens next.
This is exactly what the Mediator Pattern does.
Without the pattern:
Every component is tangled with every other. Add one new component and you update everyone.
With Mediator:

// Everyone only talks to the mediator
mediator.notify(this, "changed");

blocks.content: Components know only the mediator. The mediator knows the rules. Add a new component only the mediator needs updating.
It is useful when:

["Multiple components need to react to each other's changes.","You want to centralize coordination logic in one place.","You want components to be reusable without being hardwired to specific peers."]
items: Multiple components need to react to each other's changes.
You want to centralize coordination logic in one place.
You want components to be reusable without being hardwired to specific peers.

blocks.content: Let's walk through a real example and see how it works.
1. The Problem: Tightly Coupled Chat Room
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Tightly Coupled Chat Room

blocks.content: Imagine you are building a chat room system. The room has several participants Alice, Bob, and Charlie. Each participant can send messages to others.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245818271-3330b504.png
In the naive approach each participant holds direct references to every other participant they want to talk to.
Naive Approach

codes.python:
class ChatUser:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.contacts = []

    def add_contact(self, user):
        self.contacts.append(user)

    def send_message(self, message):
        print(f"{self.name} sends: {message}")
        for contact in self.contacts:
            contact.receive_message(self.name, message)

    def receive_message(self, from_, message):
        print(f"{self.name} received from {from_}: {message}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    alice = ChatUser("Alice")
    bob = ChatUser("Bob")
    charlie = ChatUser("Charlie")

    # Everyone wired to everyone
    alice.add_contact(bob)
    alice.add_contact(charlie)
    bob.add_contact(alice)
    bob.add_contact(charlie)
    charlie.add_contact(alice)
    charlie.add_contact(bob)

    alice.send_message("Hey everyone!")
    bob.send_message("Hi Alice!")

blocks.content: Why This Breaks Down

1. Tight Coupling Every participant directly references every other participant. Alice knows Bob and Charlie. Bob knows Alice and Charlie. Add a fourth user Dave and you must update every existing user to add Dave as a contact.
2. Poor Scalability With 3 users you need 6 connections. With 10 users you need 90 connections. The number of connections grows as N×(N-1) it explodes fast.
3. No Central Control Want to add a rule like "muted users cannot send messages" or "log every message"? You must add that logic to every single ChatUser class.
4. No Reusability ChatUser is hardwired to talk to other ChatUser objects directly. You cannot reuse it in a different context without dragging all its dependencies with it.
5. Violates Single Responsibility ChatUser manages its own data AND manages the coordination of who talks to whom. Two very different responsibilities in one class.
What We Really Need

["Each user should only know how to send and receive messages nothing else.","All coordination logic who gets notified, who is muted, logging should live in one central place.","Adding or removing a user should require zero changes to existing users."]
items: Each user should only know how to send and receive messages nothing else.
All coordination logic who gets notified, who is muted, logging should live in one central place.
Adding or removing a user should require zero changes to existing users.

blocks.content: This is exactly what the Mediator Pattern is designed to solve.
2. The Mediator Pattern
The Mediator Pattern promotes loose coupling by centralizing communication between objects. Instead of components referring to each other directly, they all communicate through a single mediator.
Two characteristics define it:

1. Centralized communication All interaction logic lives in one place the mediator. Components never call methods on each other. When a component changes, it notifies the mediator, and the mediator coordinates the response. The complex web of many-to-many connections gets replaced by a simple star topology with the mediator at the center.

2. Loose coupling between components Each component depends only on the mediator interface not on any other component. Components can be added, removed, or replaced without modifying each other. The mediator is the only class that knows the full set of participants and how they interact.

Real-World Analogy

Think about an air traffic control tower.

Planes approaching an airport do not talk to each other to negotiate landing order or runway assignments that would be chaos with dozens of planes in the air. Instead every pilot talks only to the control tower.

The tower knows the position, speed, and fuel status of every plane and coordinates them: "Flight 237, hold at 5,000 feet. Flight 412, cleared for runway 28L."

The tower is the mediator. Planes are the components. A new plane enters the airspace the tower handles it. A plane diverts the tower adjusts. The other planes never need to know.

blocks.content: Class Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245818364-bbb83b18.png
The Four Participants
Mediator Interface ChatMediator Declares the contract for communication sendMessage() and addUser(). Every component depends only on this interface, never on concrete components.

Concrete Mediator ChatRoom Implements ChatMediator and contains all coordination logic. Holds references to every user and decides who gets notified and how. This class is intentionally allowed to know about everyone it absorbs the coupling that would otherwise be spread across all components.
Abstract Component User Holds a reference to the mediator and provides send() and receive() methods. Never holds references to other users.
Concrete Component ChatUser Sends messages by calling mediator.sendMessage() and receives messages via receive(). Completely unaware of any other user in the room.
3. How It Works
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245818553-059e7ef0.png
Step 1 The client creates a ChatRoom mediator and registers all users with it.
Step 2 When Alice wants to send a message she calls send() on herself not on Bob or Charlie directly.
Step 3 send() delegates to mediator.sendMessage(message, this). Alice notifies the mediator that is all she does.
Step 4 The ChatRoom mediator receives the message and loops through its user list. It calls receive() on every user except the sender.
Step 5 Bob and Charlie receive the message without Alice ever knowing they exist. Adding a fourth user Dave means registering him with ChatRoom. Alice, Bob, and Charlie are completely unaffected.
4. Implementing Mediator Pattern
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245819183-67f3185e.png
Let's refactor the Chat Room system step by step.
Step 1: Define the Mediator Interface
Step 2: Define the Abstract Component
Step 3: Implement Concrete Components
Step 4: Implement the Concrete Mediator
ChatRoom is the only class that knows about all users. It absorbs all the coordination logic so components stay clean.

blocks.content: Notice how adding Dave required zero changes to Alice, Bob, or Charlie. No user holds a reference to any other user. All coordination lives inChatRoom.
If we want to add a rule like "muted users cannot send" or "log every message" we change onlyChatRoom.
What We Achieved
Loose Coupling No user holds a reference to any other user. Every user only knows the mediator. Alice has no idea Bob or Charlie exist and does not need to.
Centralized Coordination All routing logic lives in ChatRoom. Want to add "muted users cannot send" or "log every message"? Change only ChatRoom zero changes to any user class.
Easy to Extend Adding Dave required registering one new user with the mediator. Alice, Bob, and Charlie were completely untouched. This is the Open/Closed Principle in action.
Scales Cleanly The naive approach needed N×(N-1) direct connections. With the mediator every user needs exactly one connection to ChatRoom. Ten users means ten connections instead of ninety.

Reusable Components ChatUser is no longer hardwired to specific peers. The same class works in any chat room, any context, with any set of participants because it depends only on the ChatMediator interface.
Separation of Concerns Each user focuses only on sending and receiving. The mediator focuses only on coordination. Neither bleeds into the other's responsibility.
